summary:
Houston, We Have a Budget is a browser-based mission-design game that turns failed attempts into opportunities to learn. Players plan a robotic lunar flyby with a limited budget, choose scientific instruments and communication capacity, experiment with engine-burn timing, and decide which data to transmit to Earth. A mission succeeds when its choices work together: reaching the target is only part of the challenge.
Our distinctive feature is a collection of failures linked to scientific explanations, short questions, and hints for the next attempt. Pixel art and immediate feedback make engineering trade-offs approachable for young people and curious beginners. NASA mission-design resources and Apollo 8 references inform the educational content, while the website identifies the simulation's simplifications and invented game values.
We developed a playable prototype and public project website. Our aim is to encourage curiosity about space engineering and show that understanding a mistake can be valuable progress.
details:
What we developed

Houston, We Have a Budget is a single-player educational game and public website created for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Our playable prototype follows a robotic lunar flyby from resource planning through a simplified flight exercise to the return of scientific observations. It runs in a browser without an account or installation.

How it works

Players begin with 100 fictional mission credits. They choose a camera or spectrometer and reserve a communication window. These decisions have consequences later: a spectrometer with a short contact window costs 95 credits, but its scientific data plus spacecraft health information require six transmission slots, while that window provides only four. Choosing the standard window brings the cost to 100 credits and supplies the six slots needed.

Next, players experiment with engine burns in a two-dimensional flight simulation. A predicted coast path and telemetry provide feedback about timing and fuel. After reaching the flyby corridor, players allocate limited communication capacity to send spacecraft health information and scientific observations to Earth. A final report explains the result and lets them retry relevant stages.

Failure is part of the learning design. Six decision and flight failure outcomes connect to six collectible concept cards. Players read an explanation, answer a short question, and earn a hint they can apply on another attempt. A relaxed mode removes the decision countdown, and a clearly labeled guided flight demonstrates one successful input sequence.

Creativity and intended impact

The project combines pixel art, mission decisions, and a collection of mistakes that becomes a record of learning. Its central idea is that a failed mission can still produce useful understanding. The budget and data-return mechanics also show why mission design requires considering how different systems depend on each other.

We designed the experience for young people and curious beginners, with potential use in classroom discussions about engineering trade-offs. Our intended impact is greater confidence in experimentation and curiosity about space careers. We have not yet measured learning outcomes or conducted a study with children.

NASA resources and scientific boundaries

NASA's Design and Develop Science Missions resource informed goal-first planning and the relationship between spacecraft, ground operations, and scientific results. Build It Yourself: Satellite! informed the connection between science objectives and instrument choices. NASA Mission Visualization and Apollo 8 records provided orbital and historical context. Our source page identifies these contributions and links the references to the game's concepts.

The flight exercise uses Earth-centered gravity, prograde thrust, and a stationary lunar target. It omits lunar gravity and does not simulate capture into lunar orbit. Distances, elapsed time, costs, and data volumes use illustrative game values rather than calibrated NASA mission parameters. NASA resources support the teaching content; this prototype does not process a NASA observational dataset or run GMAT.

Tools, implementation, and current scope

We used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas, and browser localStorage. The design process included Figma and Affinity. ChatGPT assisted with implementation, text, and procedural visuals; the supplied design document also references a Claude artifact for the initial prototype. The public site is hosted through Porkbun, with a small WordPress adapter serving the HTML homepage at our domain root. AI-use disclosures and resource credits appear on the website.

We checked budget constraints, a successful guided flight, lesson hints, and successful and incomplete data returns. The original simulation sweep also exercised 2,254 burn combinations, reaching all five flight outcome classes; that checks reachable game outcomes, not physical accuracy. The current release implements one mission route. Additional campaign scenarios, including landing, docking, and power-management challenges, remain future development. Broader accessibility improvements and player testing are planned.
